title: Founding the New York Pops
summary: Sy Rosen, Ruth registering the name, and the first Carnegie concert after the Boston Pops cancelled.

blocks.x: The pops orchestra thing, did you spot a need for that?

No. I didn’t know what else to do. There was no more studio. I didn’t fit anyplace. I’m not much of a rocker, and I guess then what I began with was my, I don’t know, stuck in my craw, something so-called I mean — forgive me — legitimate schooling, which is still very important. There was a man who ran Carnegie Hall called Sy Rosen. And after I had my catastrophe when Lenny Bernstein had the Philharmonic and I had this two week train wreck of all time, I recorded with that orchestra. They’re still buried in a vault someplace — with the Philharmonic. Made lots of sides, never to be released, mercifully I suppose. Sy subsequently became manager of the Pittsburgh Symphony and then the Philadelphia Orchestra. And at both places after work when we’d be at the local watering hole, he would say, “Why don’t you try it again sometime?” And my wife, God bless her, registered the title New York Pops. She was so angry that I had stumbled, that she didn’t want the Philharmonic to take the name, see? She said I’ll get even. So she registered that. And we just sat there and then one morning I got a call that the Boston Pops, Arthur had played what he called his beer date, every April, for something like 26 years he had played the same Wednesday night at Carnegie Hall. Never an ad, always sold out. Typical Boston Pops program with Arthur. Then John Williams comes aboard, but he comes aboard with this colossal public relations marketing team who made him the God

of music. Well you know you can’t come to — you can but you can’t — you can’t come to New York that way, you know what I’m saying? And I think he thought that he’d come in there with the Boston Pops and he would just absolutely turn everything over. Well the press just crucified him, as they have all of us at one time or another. And he, well I think within the next couple of days, I don’t remember exactly, but he told Boston he’d never play, take the date off the schedule. And the day that call came to Carnegie, Ruth and I we have a little flat in New York, he called Ruth and myself and said, “Maybe that’s the omen, maybe you should try it again.”

Sy Rosen. This same man, Sy Rosen. He now had gone from the Pittsburgh Symphony to the Philadelphia Orchestra where he was manager, to now running Carnegie Hall. And isn’t that something? In that call he gave me a fairly stiff price what his estimate, what it would cost, and we did, as it were, a preview. We did one single concert. It began to rain at three o’clock in the afternoon, and it rained I think until four o’clock the next morning. It was like the South Pacific. But we didn’t have an empty seat. And we lost a good bit of change but it was the start of it, that’s seventeen years ago now. So strange at this time in my life to have such a golden wand of players, but it is a legitimate orchestra. It doesn’t, I mean when we start playing four to the bar I just want to run out of the house. I try to get a small group maybe interspersed from time to time.
